Interview avec Jessey Charles, fondatric: Interview with Jessey Charles, founder of an organization supporting racialized single mothers
À l’approche de la fête des Mères, il y: With Mother’s Day approaching, some initiatives hit closer to home than others, and La Maison de Débora is one of them.
L’organisme propose plus qu’un simple so: The organization offers more than just support to young moms – it’s a true space for healing. Its founder, Jessey Charles, radiates a gentle strength. She draws on her own experience to support other women. At La Maison de Débora, trauma is neither ignored nor downplayed: it is welcomed and addressed.
« Il y a beaucoup de tabous dans la comm: “There are a lot of taboos in the Black community,” Jessey points out. Repressing, keeping quiet, bottling things up – all of it makes you sick, she says. With determination, she creates spaces for talking and mutual support, outings, workshops, moments of respite – so many opportunities to break isolation, help people open up and begin rebuilding from the ground up.
J’ai eu la chance de rencontrer Jessey,: I had the chance to meet Jessey, as well as one of the young mothers she supports.
<strong><em>La fête des Mères provoque p: Mother’s Day can sometimes bring on a sense of loneliness for some of these moms. Aware of the isolation these women can experience during motherhood, La Maison de Débora reaches out to young racialized mothers. Founded by Jessey Charles, a nurse and community worker in Rivière-des-Prairies, the organization offers a refuge where people can speak freely, where confidence is reborn and where women learn to get back on their feet. Its goal? “To break the cycle of generational trauma and allow these women to go from surviving to living.”
<strong>Rivière-des-Prairies,</strong> u: Rivière-des-Prairies, on a busy Thursday morning. In Jessey Charles’s small office, bags of donations are piled up, spilling over into the entryway. Children’s coats, boots and carefully sorted clothes await their next destination. “We’re putting together a bazaar for families in Montréal-Nord, especially newcomers. We collect, we sort, we hand out,” she explains, focused, behind her constantly buzzing phone. Parents, teenagers, young mothers – they all know they can count on her.
À 41 ans, Jessey a une énergie débordant: At 41, Jessey has boundless energy. Thick glasses, hoop earrings and a ponytail pulled back tight, her style is decidedly youthful. More than a community worker, she is a nurse by training. She spent several years working in Montréal CLSCs before answering a deeper calling: community work. “Sometimes I tell myself I picked the wrong career. I should have been a social worker,” she confides.
En 2014, Jessey fonde <l1>La Maison de D: In 2014, Jessey founded <l1>La Maison de Débora</l1>, an organization that supports racialized single mothers aged 16 to 41. The name she chose is no accident: “Deborah, in the Bible, is a judge, a warrior, a leader. A figure of strength. That’s what I want for these women: for them to rise up and become pillars.”
Qu’elles soient enceintes ou jeunes mama: Whether they’re pregnant or young moms, these women have the opportunity to be supported for a year. La Maison de Débora is currently helping about 20 of them. Some receive close follow-up, while others are seen more occasionally, Jessey explains. “For a long time, we weren’t able to offer structured follow-up because of various obstacles,” she says. She mentions, in particular, a lack of funding. The organization recently secured funding that finally allows it to lay solid foundations and formally structure itself.
Grâce à La Maison de Débora, Jessey acco: Through La Maison de Débora, Jessey supports these women day to day. “As soon as a need comes up,” she continues, “we listen to them, we meet all their immediate needs and, beyond that, we also offer activities that bring people together; it helps them flourish.”
Des ateliers de cuisine où on parle auta: Cooking workshops where there’s as much talking as eating, talks, family outings and also supportive therapy sessions are on offer. “Some have been abused, many are living with deep trauma. Being young, a mother and racialized is an intersectionality that isolates them even more. We have to give them the chance to reclaim their identity,” she says.
Ce combat, Jessey le mène aussi en écho: Jessey’s fight also echoes her own life. “My mother got pregnant young. She didn’t have any support, and I saw the consequences it had on her personal life. She suffered, and so did I, as a result.” The community worker speaks gently but frankly about the wounds left by a loving mother who became vulnerable after falling into depression. “She put me down without meaning to. She loved me, but illness makes you say things you would never say otherwise…So that strengthened my desire to serve those moms even more,” she says.
Alors, pour Jessey, aider ces jeunes mèr: So for Jessey, helping these young mothers also means helping their children grow up better. “They need to be able to heal from their own trauma so they don’t pass it on,” she concludes.
<strong>« Ça fait toute une différence q: “It makes all the difference when someone believes in you!”
<strong>Le mardi suivant notre première: The Tuesday after our first meeting, it’s 9 a.m. when we meet Jessey again in a sun-drenched apartment in Ahuntsic. Facing her, focused, Jeanne Rosebertha St Fort, 28, mother of a two-year-old girl, gently wields brushes and concealer. Tonight, Jessey will host an episode of the podcast Le Tournant, and it’s this mom, whom she has been supporting for several months, who’s in charge of her makeup.
« C’est grâce à La Maison de Débora que: “It’s thanks to La Maison de Débora that I was able to take this path seriously,” says Jeanne, visibly shy but speaking with confidence. Thanks to Jessey, she landed her very first paid contract as a makeup artist. A small contract on the surface, but one that allowed her to rebuild a self-confidence she thought she had lost.
« La Maison de Débora a été un pilier po: “La Maison de Débora has been a pillar for me as a single mom,” she continues. “I went through things that I brushed off for a long time. Traumas that I normalized, as if they were normal. I’ve always known loneliness, but it was really when I became a mother that I realized what I’d been through.”
Elle marque une pause et dépose son pinc: She pauses and sets down her brush. “In my family, I’ve always been the black sheep. The rebel. But they don’t know what I went through. They don’t know what my father said, what he did. He was violent with my mother, violent with me. There are things you should never hear from a parent’s mouth…”
Le silence s’allonge quelques secondes,: The silence stretches for a few seconds, then she picks her brush back up. “I can’t wait to tell my story. Even if it makes people uncomfortable. Because we shouldn’t have to keep our emotions quiet so we don’t hurt others.”
Car c’est bien en parlant que la jeune f: Because it was by talking that the young woman began to heal, she acknowledges. She remembers her first moment with La Maison de Débora: a simple apple-picking outing. “There were a bunch of us moms, my daughter and me. That day, I understood that I wasn’t alone.”
Depuis, les choses ont évolué. Lentement: Since then, things have changed. Slowly but surely. “That’s when I offered my makeup services to Jessey. And every time we met, she talked to me, she listened to me, she encouraged me. Even when I doubted myself, she’d tell me: ‘Go for it, I believe in you.’ And honestly… it makes all the difference when someone believes in you!”
La jeune mère n’oubliera jamais cette ma: The young mother will never forget that helping hand. Nor will she forget the hardest moments: “When I didn’t even have enough to buy diapers, La Maison de Débora was there. Jessey is truly a support for me…”
<strong>« Il y a beaucoup de tabous dans: “There are a lot of taboos in the Black community”
Jeanne lève les yeux, comme pour cherche: Jeanne looks up, as if searching for her words in a corner of the ceiling. Then she gently continues: “My mother went through a lot. Too much, even, and she learned to hide her emotions. And I did the same.”
Ses mains bougent légèrement, comme pour: Her hands move slightly, as if to underline the intensity of what she’s sharing. “Everything built up over the years. And then, when my daughter was born, it exploded. I had postpartum depression. It was like everything I had buried blew up in my face all at once.”
Jessey hoche la tête, elle prend la paro: Jessey nods and takes her turn to speak. “We know that in the Black community, talking about certain things is complicated. Incest, as well as physical or psychological abuse, are seen as things that don’t affect a human being. But they do. We’re afraid of how others will see us, afraid of dragging the family name through the mud, afraid of being rejected. There’s so much left unsaid, so many secrets kept to protect the family’s honour. But at what cost?”
Elle poursuit : « Il y a beaucoup de bia: She continues: “There are a lot of biases in our culture. When you’re not doing well mentally or emotionally, you’re seen as weak. As if vulnerability were something to be ashamed of.”
C’est cette mentalité-là que Jessey veut: It’s this mindset that Jessey wants to break down through her work with these moms. She insists, keeping her eyes closed so the young woman can do her eyelids. “Repressing your emotions is dangerous. That silence makes us sick. This lack of vulnerability means we store up our emotions; it comes out in different physical and mental illnesses,” she concludes.
“It’s time we broke these silences. It’s time we stopped surviving in silence,” she says.
Le maquillage est presque terminé, et Je: The makeup is almost done, and Jessey is ready for this new day. Before leaving, she makes a point of addressing young girls, looking straight into the camera: “Get to know yourself. When you know who you are, you make choices that protect you, you’re less influenced by your environment. It’s by standing firm in your identity that you move in the right direction.” She smiles, then concludes: “You’re beautiful just the way you are. Don’t conform to society’s standards. Love yourself the way you were created. You can enhance what you have, yes, but remember: the first person who has to love you is you.”
